title: Designing GIS Interfaces People Can Actually Use
excerpt: Good GIS software turns complex spatial data into a clear next action. The interface has to respect the map, the workflow, and the person making the decision.
content:
## The job of a GIS interface

A strong GIS interface does more than put data on a map. It helps someone inspect a place, understand what changed, compare the right details, and decide what to do next.

### What matters

- Keep map interactions close to the user task.
- Make selected features, related records, attachments, and imagery easy to inspect.
- Preserve context when users move between map, table, dashboard, and field workflows.
- Treat performance and readability as part of the product, not polish at the end.

### Where I focus

My work is strongest where spatial data, operational constraints, and user interface decisions meet: ArcGIS applications, parcel tools, dashboards, mobile map workflows, and Python-backed data pipelines.

title: Why ArcGIS Workflows Need Safer Change Paths
excerpt: Maps and configurations change constantly. Safer clone, diff, validation, and review paths make those changes easier to trust.
content:
## Change is part of the map

ArcGIS web maps often carry operational meaning: layers, popups, renderers, filters, fields, relationships, and access settings. When those configurations change, teams need a way to understand what changed and recover when something goes wrong.

### A safer pattern

- Work on copies before touching production maps.
- Compare configuration changes before pushing them forward.
- Validate credentials, environments, and target maps early.
- Document the first-user path so adoption does not depend on tribal knowledge.

### Why it matters

The goal is not to make GIS teams think like software teams. It is to give them enough version-control behavior to protect real map workflows.

title: From Spatial Data To Decision Support
excerpt: Parcel records, GPS data, elevation surfaces, and dashboards become useful when they are shaped around a decision someone needs to make.
content:
## Data becomes useful through shape

Spatial software has to translate raw inputs into something someone can inspect. That might be a parcel detail view, a mobile course map, an elevation surface, a related-record panel, or a dashboard showing the state of a workflow.

### The pattern

- Start with the decision or field workflow.
- Keep the data path understandable.
- Make uncertainty and constraints visible.
- Build interfaces that work across desktop, dashboard, and mobile contexts.

### The result

The best geospatial tools feel calm because the complexity is handled in the right layer: data pipelines, API contracts, map rendering, and interface design all serving the same user task.
